Wind
wind
n. (rendering Hebrew ruach, Greek anemos/pneuma)
From Saxon wind, cognate with Latin ventus. In both biblical tongues the word for wind is also the word for breath and for spirit — Hebrew ruach, Greek pneuma — so that the natural fact and the supernatural Person are named together, and Scripture repeatedly moves between the two in a single sentence.

Biblical Definition

Wind is the standing figure for what is real, powerful, and beyond human management. The Lord Jesus uses it to explain the new birth to a ruler who wanted a mechanism: “The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth: so is every one that is born of the Spirit” (John 3:8) — the effects are unmistakable and the cause is sovereign and unseen. At Pentecost the figure becomes a sign: “suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting” (Acts 2:2). The same word describes emptiness and judgment: “they have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind” (Hosea 8:7) — sin returns with interest and in kind. And James uses it for the unstable soul: the doubter “is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed” (James 1:6). Taken together the uses set an antithesis. There is a wind that blows where it will and gives life, and there is a wind a man sows and is destroyed by; there is a Spirit who fills a house, and there is a gust that drives a man who will not be anchored. What no use of the figure ever allows is that the wind might be produced, steered, or scheduled by the men it moves.

Webster 1828 Definition

Air in motion; a current of air; by figure, breath, spirit, and also that which is empty or unstable. In Scripture, the wind that bloweth where it listeth as an image of the new birth, the rushing mighty wind of Pentecost, sowing the wind and reaping the whirlwind, and the doubter driven with the wind and tossed.

expand to see more

WIND, n. 1. Air in motion with any degree of velocity, from the gentlest breeze to the most violent storm.

2. Breath; power of respiration.

3. Anything insignificant or light as wind; empty words; vanity.

4. From Saxon wind; Latin ventus. Hebrew ruach and Greek pneuma denote wind, breath, and spirit alike.

5. In Scripture, the wind bloweth where it listeth, John 3; they have sown the wind, Hos. 8.

Key Scripture

John 3:8 — "The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth: so is every one that is born of the Spirit."

Acts 2:2 — "And suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting."

Hosea 8:7 — "For they have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind: it hath no stalk: the bud shall yield no meal: if so be it yield, the strangers shall swallow it up."

James 1:6 — "But let him ask in faith, nothing wavering. For he that wavereth is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed."

Modern Corruption

The Spirit's sovereign freedom is either domesticated into a technique that can produce revival on demand, or spiritualised into a vague and undoctrinal atmosphere that no longer requires the new birth at all.

expand to see more

John 3:8 was spoken to a man who wanted a method, and the answer withholds one. The wind blows where it listeth; Nicodemus cannot arrange it, and neither can the church. The revivalist tradition after Finney reversed this deliberately, teaching that a revival is not a miracle but the right use of the appointed means — which in practice meant techniques for producing decisions, and produced a century of manufactured awakenings with little fruit. The charismatic wing repeats the error with different machinery, working the room until something happens and calling the result the Spirit. Both make the wind a thing men raise. Scripture leaves the church with means she is commanded to use — preaching, prayer, the ordinances, holy living — and leaves the wind with God, which is exactly why revival is asked for and never engineered.

The opposite corruption empties the figure. Where spirit becomes a vague word for atmosphere, uplift, or the better part of human nature, the new birth ceases to be a supernatural act and becomes a change of outlook, and men are told they need encouragement rather than resurrection. The Lord's words to Nicodemus close that door: except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God, and the birth is of the Spirit, not of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man. The principle to recover holds both truths without compromise. The Spirit is sovereign and unmanageable, so no man may claim to produce Him; and He is really and powerfully at work, so no man may reduce Him to a mood.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ruach, wind, breath, or spirit; se'arah, a whirlwind or tempest; Greek anemos, wind, and pneuma, wind, breath, or the Holy Ghost.

expand to see more

Hebrew ruach (H7307) — wind, breath, spirit; the single word covering the east wind, the breath of life, and the Spirit of God.

Hebrew se'arah (H5591) — a whirlwind or tempest; the whirlwind that took Elijah up and the one out of which God answered Job.

Greek anemos (G417) — wind; the winds Christ rebuked on the sea (Matthew 8:26) and the winds of doctrine (Ephesians 4:14).

Greek pneuma (G4151) — wind, breath, spirit; the word used twice in John 3:8, of the wind and of the Spirit.

Greek pnoē (G4157) — a blowing or breath; “a rushing mighty wind” at Pentecost (Acts 2:2).

Usage

"Of the sovereignty of the new birth: The wind bloweth where it listeth... so is every one that is born of the Spirit (John 3:8)."

"Of judgment in kind and in measure: they have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind (Hosea 8:7)."

"Of the unstable soul: like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed (James 1:6)."
